The Gravity Factor: Super-Earths (the most common planet type) are physically superior at holding onto their "habitability budget" than low-mass bodies like Mars. In systems where these are the norm, the 4% frequency for moderate atmospheres is likely more stable and robust than our own.

Quantity vs. Quality: The 4% represents our quantity bracket—the frequency of available "shells." The 2 billion figure represents our quality bracket—how many of those shells are currently "furnished" with an oxygen-rich atmosphere at this exact snapshot in time.

The "Subsurface" Expansion
If we include ice-capped ocean worlds in our "Good Target" count, the statistics for our 100-body Standard Kit shift significantly:
From 4% to 10%: In our local grab, we have at least 5 or 6 bodies (Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Enceladus, Titan, and potentially Pluto or Ceres) that likely harbor liquid water beneath an ice shell. This moves our "Workable Target" count from 4% to roughly 10% of the total population.
The Ultimate "Cave" Strategy: We previously discussed niche habitability in terms of deep basins (Valles Marineris). An ice-capped ocean is the ultimate literal version of this—a globally shielded, thermally stable, and chemically rich "basement" that is entirely independent of stellar flux or atmospheric loss.

Adding these worlds changes our System Habitability Index (SHI) from a "Peak and Tail" model to a "Multi-Floor" model:
The Penthouse (1%): The Oxygen-rich "Ideal" target (Earth).
The Middle Floors (3%): The "Moderate Atmosphere" near-misses (Mars, Venus, Titan).
The Basements (6%): The Ice-Capped Ocean worlds. These are the "silver needles" that don't need a golden sun; they rely on tidal heating and radiolysis.

If 10% of our local 100-body grab offers some form of liquid-water utility, then the galactic average for habitability is much more robust than we first thought. Even in a "Near-Miss Desert" where no planet has an atmosphere, the system is still statistically likely to host several "Subsurface Oases."
This means that while finding a place to stand without a suit is rare, finding liquid water is a standard, baseline outcome for almost any system in the 10-trillion-body census. We haven't just found a few caves; we've realized that the "92% Negligible" population is actually a massive geochemical warehouse where the "habitability budget" is stored in deep-freeze.
Analogy: If an Earth-like world is a furnished mansion, and a Mars-like world is a sturdy shell, then an ice-capped ocean is a high-end fallout shelter.
